title: Your PQC Migration Plan May Be Missing the Systems That Matter Most
summary: Migrating an application to post-quantum cryptography isn’t complete if connected systems still use vulnerable encryption; network visibility reveals hidden dependencies, helping teams scope migration across entire communication paths.
body_markdown:
Your team upgrades a customer-facing application to support[post-quantum cryptography (PQC)](https://www.netscout.com/what-is/post-quantum-cryptography-pqc) . The new encryption works, testing is complete, and the application is marked as migrated.


But what happens when that application connects to an internal database that still relies on quantum-vulnerable cryptography?


The application may meet its migration requirements while sensitive information continues moving through connections that have not been assessed.


This is an important challenge in PQC migration. Organizations need to understand the cryptographic dependencies surrounding their applications before they can determine the full scope of the work.


## The Hidden Dependencies Behind an Application


Enterprise applications rarely operate independently. A customer transaction might pass through an API gateway, application server, authentication service, and database before processing is complete.


Each connection can have its own encryption configuration, software dependencies, and technology owner.


Consider an[online banking application](https://www.netscout.com/industries/financial-services) . Its public-facing connection may use quantum-resistant key establishment, while an internal service still negotiates a traditional elliptic-curve key exchange. Upgrading the external connection would leave that internal communication dependent on cryptography vulnerable to future quantum attacks.


The complication is ownership. The application team may manage the front end, infrastructure may manage the database, and another team may maintain authentication services. Without understanding how those systems communicate, migration plans can overlook dependencies that cross organizational boundaries.


## Why a Cryptographic Inventory May Be Incomplete


A cryptographic inventory documents the algorithms, protocols, certificates, and systems that use cryptography. It helps organizations identify what requires migration and assign responsibility.


However, inventories built primarily from application documentation, asset records, or configuration reviews may not capture every communication path.


An application diagram may show a database dependency without identifying the cryptography negotiated between the systems. A legacy service may still communicate with an application even though it no longer appears in current architecture documentation.


The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) recognizes cryptographic discovery and inventory as foundational activities for PQC migration planning.


The challenge is establishing which cryptographic technologies are actually operating, where they are used, and which dependencies could complicate changes.


## How Network Visibility Strengthens PQC Readiness


Observing real network communications provides additional evidence for assessing cryptographic usage. For supported traffic, network analysis can reveal details such as protocol versions, negotiated algorithms, and communicating systems. These observations help security teams identify dependencies that warrant closer examination and compare actual network behavior with existing inventories.


NETSCOUT[Omnis Cyber Intelligence](https://www.netscout.com/product/cyber-intelligence) supports this process through[deep packet inspection](https://www.netscout.com/deep-packet-inspection) and packet-derived intelligence. For supported, observed communications, it can provide visibility into encryption characteristics and help identify where traditional cryptography remains in use, including certain non-PQC TLS 1.3 key exchanges. This evidence complements application discovery and configuration analysis.


## Plan Migration Around the Full Communication Path


Before declaring an application migrated, security and infrastructure teams should examine the systems it communicates with and the cryptographic protections used along those connections. That means identifying relevant dependencies, confirming ownership, assessing where quantum-vulnerable cryptography remains, and validating changes after implementation.


A useful starting question for the migration team is: If we upgrade this application, which connected systems will continue using quantum-vulnerable cryptography?


Answering it can expose work that an application-by-application migration plan would otherwise miss, helping teams establish more accurate priorities and avoid discovering critical dependencies late in the transition.
